rules.rule_en: Finite verbs act as a main verb, indicate number, person and tense, and agree with the subject.
Non-finite verbs (verbals) do not act as a verb, do not indicate number, person, or tense, and act as nouns, adjectives, or adverbs.
Gerunds are formed by adding -ing to the verb (V+ing) and act as nouns.
Infinitives are formed by adding 'to' before the verb (to+V).
Present participles are formed by adding -ing to the verb (V+ing) and can be used as adjectives.
Past participles are formed using the V3 form of the verb.
Perfect participles are formed by 'having' + V3.
The infinitive is often called 'to + verb'.
Infinitives may be used without 'to' after modals (shall, will, do, did, would, make, need, may, might, could, must, let, dare, see) called Bare Infinitives.
Infinitives can function as subject, direct object, subject complement, adjective, or adverb.
A gerund is an action word ending in -ing that functions as a noun.
Gerunds are used as subjects, objects, complements, objects to a preposition, in compound nouns, and in opposition to a pronoun.
Gerunds are used after phrasal verbs composed of 'verb + preposition' (e.g., look forward to, give up, take to).
Gerunds are used after specific verbs: enjoy, finish, keep, mind, suggest, forgive, excuse, postpone, go.
Gerunds are used after phrases like 'It's no use', 'It's no good'.
Words like 'begin', 'love', 'continue', 'try', 'learn', 'start', 'neglect' can be followed by an infinitive or gerund.
When infinitive or gerund is used after 'stop', they mean different things.
Participles come after an object to describe it and express the state the object is in.
Present participle indicates an activity that is continuing and is in progress.
A present or past participle can function as an adjective phrase to describe a noun placed before it.
A Gerund is a verb form ending in -ing that functions as a noun.
Infinitives are formed by 'to' + base verb, functioning as subjects, objects, or modifiers.
Participles (Present -ing, Past -ed/-en) function as adjectives or parts of verb phrases.
Finite verbs are limited by person, number, and tense; Non-finite verbs are not.
Finite verbs change tense and number according to the subject.
Non-finite verbs have no subject and do not change according to the tense or number.
Non-finite verbs (verbals) do not indicate tense and are classified into gerunds, infinitives, and participles.
The infinitive is formed using 'to + verb'.
Plain or bare infinitives are used without 'to' after modals and specific verbs (shall, will, do, did, would, make, need, may, might, could, must, let, dare, see).
An infinitive can function as a subject, direct object, subject complement, adjective, or adverb.
A Gerund phrase consists of a gerund plus modifier(s), object(s), and/or complement(s).
Use gerunds after verbs: 'enjoy', 'finish', 'keep', 'mind', 'suggest', 'forgive', 'excuse', 'postpone', 'go'.
Gerunds are used after a preposition.
Gerunds describe a real action.
Use infinitives after verbs: 'like', 'refuse'.
Infinitives are used to describe a general or future action.
Infinitives are used to express 'reason', 'intention', or 'purpose'.
After verbs like 'begin', 'love', 'continue', 'try', 'learn', 'start', 'neglect', you can use either gerunds or infinitives.
The meaning changes when using a gerund versus an infinitive after the verb 'stop'.
Use gerunds after the phrases 'It's no use' and 'It's no good'.
Verbs which have the past or the present form are called FINITE verbs; they change with tense.
Verbs which do not change to indicate tense, number, or person are called NON-FINITE verbs.
Infinitives are the base form of the verb, often preceded by 'to'. They function as noun phrases or modifiers.
Participles are formed by adding 'ing' or 'ed' to the base verb and are used as adjectives to modify a noun.
A Gerund is a verb that ends in ‘ing’ and is used as a noun. It can function as the subject of a verb, the object of a verb, or the object of a preposition.
Non-finite verbs (verbals) do not show tense and do not function as a verb in the sentence.
Gerunds end in -ing and function as nouns.
Infinitives consist of 'to' + base form of a verb and function as nouns, adjectives, or adverbs.
Participles end in -ing (present) or -ed, -d, -t, -en, -n (past) and function as adjectives.
Gerunds function as nouns and end in -ing.
Infinitives are the base form of a verb preceded by 'to'.
Finite verbs indicate tense, time of actions, and change according to the subject (number or person).
Non-finite verbs (verbals) do not indicate tense or time and do not change according to the subject.
Gerund: Verb + ing used as a noun.
Infinitive: Formed as 'to + verb' (to-infinitive). Functions as a noun, adjective, or adverb.
Bare infinitive: Infinitive used without 'to' after modals (Shall, Will, Do, Did, Would, Make, Need, May, Might, Could, Must, Let, Dare, See).
Participle: Verb + ing (present) or -ed/-d/-t/-en/-n (past). Functions as an adjective or verbal adjective.
Present participles (e.g., hearing, thinking) indicate an unfinished action.
Sentences are determined by finite verbs (e.g., saw, spoke, rushed, cried).
Past participles (e.g., driven, loaded, stricken) indicate a completed action and usually end with -ed, -d, -n, -t, or -en.
Present and past participles are used as adjectives to qualify nouns.
Infinitives are 'to + present form of the verb'.
Bare infinitives give the same meaning of an infinitive without the use of 'to'.
Gerunds are verbal nouns. It is 'verb+ing'.
A participle is used as part of the continuous form of a verb.
A participle is used as an adjective (verbal adjective).
